seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about civil engineering (VRD) in Luxembourg
seo.viabilisationContent:
Site servicing in Luxembourg encompasses all roadworks and utilities (VRD — Voiries et Réseaux Divers) needed to make a plot buildable and connectable to public networks. These works represent a major budget item in any development or property promotion project.

In Luxembourg, VRD costs are influenced by topography (Gutland plateau vs Oesling hills), soil conditions, distance to existing networks and the specific requirements of each municipality. Luxembourg municipalities have significant autonomy in planning matters, leading to considerable differences in technical specifications.

The Pacte Logement 2.0 (law of 30 July 2021) and the subdivision tax reform have modified infrastructure financing mechanisms, with increased developer participation in public infrastructure costs.
seo.postesContent:
VRD works break down into several main categories:

  • Roadworks: earthworks, subbase, base course, wearing course (asphalt), kerbs, pavements, signage. Average cost: EUR 80 to 150/sqm of road surface. Municipal roads must comply with the Roads and Bridges Administration standards.
  • Water supply networks: pipelines, connections, stop valves, meters. Connection to the municipal network is subject to an infrastructure tax set by municipal regulation (EUR 1,500 to 5,000 per plot).
  • Drainage: separate system (foul water + rainwater) mandatory in new development zones. Retention basins required under the amended law of 19 December 2008 on water.
  • Dry utilities: electricity (underground network mandatory in urban areas), telecommunications (fibre optic), natural gas (Enovos/Creos). Shared trenches optimise costs.
  • Street lighting: poles, LED luminaires, cabling, control cabinets. New installations must comply with the Grand-Ducal regulation of 11 November 2022 on light pollution.
seo.coutParLotTitle: Servicing cost per plot by density
seo.coutParLotContent:
VRD cost per plot varies significantly by development density:

  • Detached houses (5-10 plots/ha): EUR 40,000 to 70,000/plot. Low density means longer network runs per plot.
  • Terraced houses (15-25 plots/ha): EUR 25,000 to 45,000/plot. Intermediate density optimises the network length/plot count ratio.
  • Apartment buildings (50-100 dwellings/ha): EUR 10,000 to 25,000/dwelling. High density pools infrastructure costs.

These ranges include primary VRD (site access) and secondary VRD (internal distribution), but exclude tertiary VRD (private facilities, parking, private landscaping).

The LISER report on land development highlights that densification is the most effective strategy for reducing infrastructure cost per dwelling.
seo.obligationsContent:
In Luxembourg, VRD obligations are governed by several texts:

  • Law of 19 July 2004 (municipal planning): defines buildable zones in the PAG and development conditions in PAPs. The developer is generally required to complete internal VRD and transfer them to the municipality after acceptance.
  • Financial contribution: the developer must contribute to public infrastructure financing (schools, green spaces, transport infrastructure). The Pacte Logement 2.0 provides for convention mechanisms between municipalities and developers.
  • Subdivision agreement: contractual document between developer and municipality setting out VRD technical specifications, completion schedule, financial guarantees (bank guarantee) and transfer conditions.
  • Infrastructure tax: each municipality sets network connection tax amounts by regulation. These taxes are added to VRD work costs.
seo.faq1Q: Who pays for VRD works in a subdivision?
seo.faq1A: In a Luxembourg subdivision, the developer generally funds all internal VRD (internal roads, distribution networks, lighting, green spaces) and contributes to external VRD (upstream network reinforcement). After acceptance, roads and networks are transferred to the municipality for maintenance. VRD costs are passed on in the sale price of plots or dwellings.
seo.faq2Q: What is the cost of connecting to public networks?
seo.faq2A: The cost depends on the municipality and network type. Water supply: EUR 1,500 to 5,000 per plot. Drainage: EUR 2,000 to 8,000. Electrical connection (Creos): EUR 2,000 to 6,000. Fibre optic (POST Luxembourg) is generally free for new construction. Total connection fees represent EUR 8,000 to 20,000 per plot.
seo.faq3Q: How to manage a sloping site for VRD?
seo.faq3A: A sloping site in Luxembourg (common in the Oesling and valleys) entails significant surcharges: retaining walls (EUR 150 to 500/sqm of facing), major earthworks, specific drainage systems, and pressure pipelines. The overall surcharge can reach 30 to 50% compared to a flat site. A prior topographic and geotechnical survey is essential.
seo.faq4Q: What is the average site servicing timeline?
seo.faq4A: Site servicing typically takes 6 to 12 months for the works themselves, excluding administrative timelines. Preparatory phases (studies, municipal approvals) can add 6 to 18 months. Provisional acceptance occurs at work completion, followed by a 1-year warranty period before final acceptance and transfer to the municipality. The total timeline is typically 18 to 36 months.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about HVAC sizing
seo.dimensionnementContent: HVAC sizing uses the EN 12831 standard adapted to Luxembourg's climate (design temperature -12 to -15 degrees C). Heating needs range from 25 kWh/m2/year (class A) to 300+ kWh/m2/year (class I).
seo.normesTitle: EN 12831 standard and Luxembourg climate conditions
seo.normesContent: Transmission and ventilation losses calculation, design temperature -12 degrees C for Luxembourg City, -15 degrees C for highland areas.
seo.pacTitle: Heat pump vs. pellets: comparison for Luxembourg
seo.pacContent: Heat pump (COP 3.0-4.0, EUR 15,000-22,000) for well-insulated buildings (A-D). Pellet boiler (85-95% efficiency, EUR 12,000-18,000) for houses with storage space. Hybrid recommended for E-I classes.
seo.vmcTitle: Heat recovery ventilation: essential for high-performance buildings
seo.vmcContent: Dual-flow HRV recovers 80-95% of exhaust heat. Cost EUR 5,000-12,000, saves 25-40% of heating needs.
seo.faq1q: How do I size my heating system?
seo.faq1a: Based on EN 12831: transmission and ventilation losses, considering surface area, insulation and Luxembourg design temperatures (-12 to -15 degrees C).
seo.faq2q: Heat pump or pellets for Luxembourg?
seo.faq2a: Heat pump for well-insulated homes (A-D), pellets for older houses with storage. Hybrid recommended for E-I.
seo.faq3q: Is HRV ventilation mandatory?
seo.faq3a: Not formally, but practically indispensable for classes A-B.
seo.faq4q: What budget for a complete HVAC system?
seo.faq4a: For 150m2: heat pump (~EUR 18,000) + HRV (~EUR 8,000) + distribution (~EUR 5,000) = ~EUR 30,000-35,000 before Klimabonus.
seo.faq5a: Insulate first, then right-size the system. Over-sizing reduces heat pump COP. Heating curve adjustment is essential.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about the hedonic model
seo.modeleTitle: The hedonic model applied to the Luxembourg market
seo.modeleContent:
The hedonic model is an econometric approach that decomposes a property's price into the sum of implicit values of its characteristics. Developed by Rosen (1974), it rests on the hypothesis that the market price reflects buyers' preferences for each housing attribute.

In Luxembourg, the Housing Observatory (Ministry of Housing / LISER) regularly publishes hedonic models calibrated on actual transactions recorded by the Registration Administration (AED). These models enable construction of quality-constant price indices, neutralising the effect of changes in the composition of properties sold.

Our implementation uses a log-linear model: ln(Price) = β0 + Σ(βi × Xi) + ε. The dependent variable is the log of price, allowing coefficients to be interpreted directly as elasticities (percentage impact). Explanatory variables cover area, location (municipality/neighbourhood), floor, general condition, CPE energy class, parking availability and outdoor amenities.
seo.coefficientsContent:
Our model coefficients are calibrated from available Luxembourg data:

  • Area: elasticity of -0.35% per additional sqm above 80 sqm. This coefficient reflects the declining marginal price per sqm with increasing area — a well-documented phenomenon in property literature.
  • Floor: ground floor suffers a discount of approximately 7%, first floor 3%. Upper floors (4+) benefit from a 3% premium, and penthouses up to 8%. Source: Housing Observatory.
  • General condition: a new or fully renovated property earns a premium of approximately 7%. A property needing cosmetic work suffers a 5% discount, and one needing full renovation 15%.
  • CPE energy class: classes A-B bring a 5% premium, while F-G carry an 8% discount. Spuerkeess has documented this gap in its Luxembourg green premium studies.
  • Parking: an indoor parking space adds approximately 5% to the dwelling price (equivalent to EUR 30,000-45,000 depending on location).
seo.sourcesContent:
The reliability of a hedonic model depends directly on the quality and representativeness of underlying data. In Luxembourg, we use several sources:

  • Housing Observatory: hedonic price indices published quarterly, based on notarial deeds transmitted by the AED. Comprehensive coverage of the residential market since 2010.
  • STATEC: housing price index (IPIL), average prices by municipality, construction statistics.
  • Municipal authorities: PAG/PAP data, building permits, cadastral information.
  • Property listings: asking prices serve as a supplementary reference but are generally 5 to 10% above actual transaction prices.

Coefficient updates are performed semi-annually to incorporate market developments.
seo.limitesTitle: Model limitations: R² and confidence interval
seo.limitesContent:
Every statistical model has limitations that must be understood:

  • R² (coefficient of determination): our model shows an R² of approximately 0.75, meaning 75% of price variance is explained by the retained variables. The remaining 25% relates to unobserved factors (view quality, natural light, noise, micro-location, common area condition).
  • Confidence interval: the point estimate is always accompanied by an interval. In dense urban areas with many transactions, the interval is ±10%. In rural areas with limited data, it can reach ±18%.
  • Atypical properties: the model is calibrated on standard properties. Luxury properties, character houses or properties with major defects may deviate significantly from the estimate.
  • Temporal effect: coefficients reflect market conditions at calibration time. During rapid market shifts, a lag may appear.
seo.faq1Q: What is the R² of the hedonic model for Luxembourg?
seo.faq1A: Our model's R² is approximately 0.75, comparable to results obtained by the Housing Observatory in its official publications. This means 75% of transaction price variance is explained by observed property characteristics (area, location, floor, condition, energy). The remaining 25% depends on unmeasurable factors such as view, noise or finish condition.
seo.faq2Q: What is the difference between a hedonic model and a property appraisal?
seo.faq2A: The hedonic model provides a statistical estimate based on market data, without a physical property visit. A property appraisal (EVS-compliant) includes an on-site inspection, thorough legal analysis (easements, planning), verification of actual condition and professional judgement. The hedonic model is ideal for initial price framing or a quick opinion of value, while an appraisal is necessary for banking operations, successions or disputes.
seo.faq3Q: Is the hedonic model applicable to commercial real estate?
seo.faq3A: Our hedonic model is calibrated primarily on the Luxembourg residential market (apartments and houses). For commercial real estate (offices, retail, logistics), income-based valuation methods (capitalisation, DCF) are more appropriate as the price depends essentially on rental yield. We offer a dedicated multi-tenant DCF tool for investment property.
seo.faq4Q: How accurate is the model by municipality?
seo.faq4A: Accuracy varies by transaction density. In Luxembourg City, Esch-sur-Alzette or Differdange, where volumes are high, the confidence interval is ±10%. In northern rural municipalities (Winseler, Kiischpelt) with fewer than 10 transactions per year, the interval can reach ±18%. The model systematically displays a confidence index adapted to each municipality.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about price indices
seo.indiceTitle: Property price indices by municipality in Luxembourg
seo.indiceContent:
The property price index by municipality is the reference tool for tracking the Luxembourg residential market. Published quarterly by the Housing Observatory in partnership with STATEC, it relies on notarial deeds registered with the AED.

In 2025, the overall index shows stabilisation after the 2022-2024 correction (-14% on average), with marked disparities between municipalities.
seo.methodologieContent:
The methodology relies on:

  • Primary source: notarial deeds registered at the AED
  • Hedonic method: price decomposition by property characteristics
  • Seasonal adjustment: X-13 ARIMA model used by STATEC
  • Smoothing: 4-quarter moving average for low-volume municipalities
seo.tendancesContent:
Municipal analysis reveals contrasting dynamics:

  • Luxembourg City: median apartment ~EUR 10,500/m2, +3% recovery in Q1-2025
  • Southern belt (Esch, Differdange): stabilisation at ~EUR 5,800-6,500/m2
  • North (Clervaux, Wiltz): slower correction, ~EUR 4,500-5,500/m2
seo.topCommunesTitle: Top municipalities: prices, yields and attractiveness
seo.topCommunesContent:
The most sought-after municipalities combine transport accessibility, quality of life and school offering:

  • Strassen, Bertrange, Hesperange: premium suburban, EUR 8,000-10,000/m2
  • Esch-sur-Alzette, Belval: secondary urban hub, ~EUR 6,000/m2
  • Mersch, Steinsel: attractive central municipalities, EUR 6,500-7,500/m2
seo.faq1q: Where do the price data per municipality come from?
seo.faq1a: Data comes from notarial deeds registered with the AED, aggregated by the Housing Observatory. These are actual transaction prices, not advertised prices.
seo.faq2q: How often are the indices updated?
seo.faq2a: Official indices are published quarterly with a 2-3 month lag. Our tool integrates the latest available data.
seo.faq3q: Why do prices differ between neighbouring municipalities?
seo.faq3a: Differences are explained by location (proximity to employment, transport), school offering, municipal taxation, and available property types.
seo.faq4q: Do the indices include new-build and existing properties?
seo.faq4a: Yes, both segments are covered. The Observatory also publishes separate indices for new (VEFA) and existing apartments.
seo.faq5q: How can I use the indices to estimate my property?
seo.faq5a: Indices provide a median price per municipality as a starting point. Then adjust for your property's specific characteristics using our estimation and comparison tools.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about PAG and PAP
seo.urbanismeTitle: Urban planning in Luxembourg: PAG and PAP
seo.urbanismeContent: Luxembourg's land planning is governed by the amended law of 19 July 2004. Each municipality has a General Development Plan (PAG) defining land use, and Particular Development Plans (PAP) detailing rules per zone.
seo.zonesTitle: Zones and buildability: understanding the rules
seo.zonesContent: Main buildable zones: HAB-1 (low density), HAB-2 (medium density), MIX (mixed use). COS and CUS coefficients define building intensity.
seo.constructibiliteContent: Assessment involves: PAG classification check, PAP rules analysis, easement verification, and feasibility study (utilities, road access).
seo.servitudesContent: Main easements: urban planning (setbacks, protected sectors), environmental (Natura 2000, flood zones), heritage (listed buildings), and private (rights of way).
seo.faq1q: Where can I view my municipality's PAG?
seo.faq1a: The PAG is available online at the Geoportail (geoportail.lu), at the town hall, or through the municipality's planning department.
seo.faq2q: What is the difference between PAG and PAP?
seo.faq2a: The PAG defines general zone allocations across the entire municipal territory. The PAP details construction rules for each specific zone or sector.
seo.faq3q: How do I know if land is buildable?
seo.faq3a: Check the PAG classification, applicable PAP rules, easements and utility availability.
seo.faq4q: What are COS and CUS?
seo.faq4a: COS is the ground coverage ratio, CUS is the total floor area ratio. They determine allowed building intensity.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about real estate AML/KYC
seo.obligationsTitle: Anti-money laundering obligations in Luxembourg real estate
seo.obligationsContent:
Anti-money laundering (AML) is a major obligation for all real estate professionals in Luxembourg. The real estate sector is identified by FATF (Financial Action Task Force) as a particularly high-risk money laundering vector due to high transaction amounts and complex ownership structures.

In Luxembourg, real estate professionals (agents, developers, property managers, valuers) have been subject to due diligence obligations since the transposition of the 4th EU AML Directive. The CSSF and the Ministry of Justice provide supervision.

Penalties for non-compliance are severe: administrative fines up to EUR 5 million or 10% of turnover, criminal sanctions (1 to 5 years imprisonment), practice bans and considerable reputational damage.
seo.loi2004Content:
The law of 12 November 2004 on combating money laundering and terrorist financing, amended several times (notably in 2018 and 2020 to transpose the 4th and 5th AML Directives), constitutes the reference legal framework:

  • Scope: any natural or legal person who, in a professional capacity, is involved in transactions relating to the purchase, sale, rental or management of real estate.
  • Main obligations: identification and verification of client and beneficial owner identity, risk assessment and management, document retention, staff training, suspicious activity reporting to the FIU.
  • Risk-based approach: enhanced due diligence measures for high-risk clients (PEPs, high-risk countries, complex structures).
  • Beneficial ownership register (RBE): companies holding real estate must register their beneficial owners with the RBE managed by Luxembourg Business Registers.
seo.identificationTitle: Client identification and enhanced due diligence
seo.identificationContent:
Identification and due diligence (KYC — Know Your Customer) measures in the Luxembourg real estate sector comprise:

  • Standard identification: identity verification (official ID, passport), address verification (utility bill, bank certificate) and source of funds verification. For legal entities: articles of association, RCS extract, identification of shareholders and beneficial owners (25% threshold).
  • Enhanced Due Diligence: mandatory for politically exposed persons (PEPs), clients resident in high-risk countries (FATF list), unusually complex or high-value transactions, and opaque ownership structures.
  • Simplified due diligence: possible for clients introduced by a fellow obliged entity, Luxembourg public institutions or companies listed on a regulated EU market.
  • Ongoing monitoring: the due diligence obligation is not limited to onboarding. The professional must regularly update KYC information and monitor transactions.
seo.declarationContent:
The reporting and sanctions framework is a pillar of the Luxembourg AML system:

  • Suspicious activity report (SAR): any professional who suspects a transaction linked to money laundering or terrorist financing must file a report with the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) of the Luxembourg Public Prosecutor's Office. The report should be filed before executing the transaction if possible.
  • Tipping-off: it is strictly prohibited to inform the client or any third party that a report has been filed (Article 5-1 of the law).
  • Administrative sanctions: fines of EUR 1,250 to 5,000,000 for legal entities. The Ministry of Justice may issue a reprimand, temporary practice ban or licence withdrawal.
  • Criminal sanctions: money laundering carries 1 to 5 years' imprisonment and a fine of EUR 1,250 to 1,250,000 (Article 506-1 of the Criminal Code). Failure to report is also criminally punishable.
  • Sanctions register: administrative sanctions are published on the Ministry of Justice website.
seo.faq1Q: Who is subject to AML obligations in Luxembourg real estate?
seo.faq1A: Subject entities include: estate agents (registered with the trade register), property developers, property managers, co-ownership syndics, notaries (for real estate transactions), lawyers (when assisting clients with property transactions), and property valuation experts. Any person professionally involved in a real estate transaction is potentially subject.
seo.faq2Q: How to identify a Politically Exposed Person (PEP)?
seo.faq2A: A PEP is a person holding or having held a prominent political, judicial or administrative function: heads of state, ministers, parliamentarians, senior judges, ambassadors, senior military officers, leaders of state-owned enterprises. Close family members and known close associates are also considered PEPs. Specialist databases (World-Check, Dow Jones) enable systematic screening.
seo.faq3Q: Is there a reporting threshold for real estate transactions?
seo.faq3A: There is no monetary threshold below which due diligence obligations do not apply. Every real estate transaction, regardless of amount, is subject to KYC obligations. However, the suspicious activity report is based on qualitative indicators (unusual client behaviour, inconsistency between profile and transaction, use of complex structures) rather than a quantitative threshold. Cash payments above EUR 10,000 are subject to a specific reporting obligation.
seo.faq4Q: How long must KYC documents be retained?
seo.faq4A: The law of 12 November 2004 requires KYC documents and information to be retained for a minimum of 5 years after the end of the business relationship or the date of the occasional transaction. Transaction documents must be kept for 5 years after execution. In practice, given Luxembourg criminal limitation periods (5 to 10 years), it is recommended to retain documents for 10 years.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about agricultural land
seo.evaluationContent: Agricultural land valuation in Luxembourg follows specific rules. Average prices range from EUR 30,000 to 80,000/ha in 2025, with peaks above EUR 100,000/ha near developable zones.
seo.prixZonesTitle: Prices by geographical zone and soil quality
seo.prixZonesContent: Prices vary by zone: Centre-South EUR 50,000-80,000/ha, Centre EUR 40,000-60,000/ha, North EUR 30,000-50,000/ha, East (Moselle) EUR 45,000-70,000/ha.
seo.facteursContent: Key factors: reclassification potential, existing rural lease (15-30% discount), existing buildings, accessibility and parcel shape.
seo.bailRuralContent: The rural lease is governed by the law of 2 July 1969, with strong tenant protections including minimum 6-year duration and pre-emption rights.
seo.faq1q: What is the average price per hectare in Luxembourg?
seo.faq1a: Between EUR 30,000 and 80,000/ha depending on zone and quality, with peaks above EUR 100,000/ha for reclassification potential.
seo.faq2q: How is soil quality assessed?
seo.faq2a: According to the Luxembourg pedological classification (classes I to V).
seo.faq3q: Does an active rural lease affect the price?
seo.faq3a: Yes, a 15-30% discount is typical due to legal tenant protections.
seo.faq4q: Can agricultural land be reclassified as buildable?
seo.faq4a: Yes, during PAG revision. Reclassification multiplies value by 10-50x but involves lengthy procedures.

vefa.interetsIntercalairesDesc: During construction, the bank releases the loan progressively. The buyer pays interest on the capital already disbursed, without repaying principal. This is the #1 hidden cost of an off-plan purchase.

vefa.garantieObligationText: The developer must provide a completion guarantee (also called extrinsic guarantee) issued by an approved financial institution in Luxembourg. This guarantee ensures the property will be completed even if the developer defaults.
vefa.garantieProtectionText: In a VEFA purchase, funds paid by the buyer are protected. The notarial deed must mention the guarantee and its conditions. Payment calls cannot exceed the percentages set by law, linked to actual construction progress.
vefa.garantieReceptionText: At delivery, the buyer may note reservations about defects found. The developer has a period to remedy them. The ten-year structural warranty covers structural defects for 10 years.
vefa.bonTvaText: The tax benefit is capped at {plafond}. Beyond that, the remaining VAT is charged at 17%. The benefit is granted only once in the buyer's lifetime and must be applied for at the Registration, Domains and VAT Administration (AED).
vefa.bonTerrainText: In a VEFA purchase, the land portion is subject to registration duties (7%), while the construction portion is subject to VAT. The split is set in the notarial deed.
vefa.bonBellegenText: Tax credit of EUR 40,000 per buyer (EUR 80,000 for a couple) on registration duties. Only applicable for the primary residence and on first use.
vefa.bonInteretsText: During the construction phase (24 to 30 months), the bank releases the loan as payment calls are made. The buyer pays monthly interest on the capital already disbursed, without amortising the principal. This often-forgotten cost typically amounts to EUR 15,000 to 25,000 for a standard loan.

seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about VEFA in Luxembourg
seo.guideTitle: Complete guide to off-plan purchases (VEFA) in Luxembourg
seo.guideContent:
VEFA (Vente en l'Etat Futur d'Achevement) is the preferred acquisition method for new housing in Luxembourg. Governed by the law of 18 April 2018, it provides a protective legal framework for buyers:

  • Reservation contract: preliminary document with maximum 5% deposit
  • Notarised sale deed: progressive ownership transfer with regulated payment calls
  • Completion guarantee: mandatory bank or insurance guarantee
  • Decennial guarantee: 10-year builder liability for hidden defects
seo.echeancierSeoContent:
Article 1601-11 sets a maximum payment schedule:

  • Sale deed: max 33%
  • Watertight stage: cumulative max 60%
  • Completion: cumulative max 95%
  • Delivery: 5% balance (retained if defects noted)
seo.tvaSeoTitle: VAT and taxation of VEFA in Luxembourg
seo.tvaSeoContent:
The VEFA tax regime offers significant advantages:

  • Land portion: 7% registration duties with Bellegen Akt for primary residence
  • Construction portion: 3% VAT (super-reduced) for primary residence, capped at EUR 50,000 in savings
  • Beyond cap or for investment: 17% VAT
seo.intercalairesTitle: Interim interest: an often underestimated cost
seo.intercalairesContent: Interim interest is paid on funds already released during construction, before capital repayment begins. For a EUR 600,000 VEFA with EUR 500,000 loan at 3.8% over 18 months of construction, interim interest is approximately EUR 12,000-15,000.
seo.faq1q: What is VEFA in Luxembourg?
seo.faq1a: VEFA is a contract where the developer sells a property not yet built or under construction. The buyer progressively becomes owner with regulated staged payments under the law of 18 April 2018.
seo.faq2q: What are the risks of VEFA?
seo.faq2a: Main risks are delivery delays (contractual penalties), specification changes (developer cannot change essential elements without agreement), and developer insolvency (covered by mandatory completion guarantee).
seo.faq3q: How do I benefit from the 3% reduced VAT rate?
seo.faq3a: The 3% rate applies to the construction portion of property intended as primary residence. The application is made to the AED, typically through the notary.
seo.faq4q: What if there are defects at delivery?
seo.faq4a: At reception, prepare a detailed report listing all defects. The 5% balance is retained until defects are fixed. The developer must correct within a reasonable timeframe.
seo.faq5a: Yes, interim interest is deductible from taxable income like mortgage interest, within the caps for primary residence (EUR 1,500-3,000/year).

vefa.retardChantierHint: If delivery is delayed, the bank has already released the full loan: intercalary interest keeps accruing on the full capital until the completion guarantee is released and amortization begins.
vefa.gfaSubtitle: Mandatory for VEFA developments. Protects buyers against developer default.
vefa.gfaPrime: GFA premium rate (% of total price)
vefa.gfaExtrinsequeNote: Premium paid to developer by buyer via sale price. Bank guarantee or insurance covering completion cost. LU standard.
vefa.gfaIntrinsequeNote: No external premium — developer proves strength (own funds ≥ 75 % of construction cost, no bank loan). Rarer, used for small projects.

seo.faqTitle: FAQ — Co-ownership Management in Luxembourg
seo.gestionTitle: Co-ownership management in Luxembourg: the role of the syndic
seo.gestionContent:
In Luxembourg, the management of a co-owned building is governed by the law of 16 May 1975 on co-ownership of buildings. Professional syndics (such as BRUNATA, Leximmo, ImmoConcept) handle the administrative, technical and financial management on behalf of the co-owners' assembly.

Their responsibilities include: preparing the budget forecast, distributing charges according to shares, maintaining common areas, arranging insurance, and keeping accounts. The syndic convenes and chairs general assemblies and implements voted decisions.

Our digital dashboard enables syndics to efficiently simulate and present energy renovation scenarios, a central challenge given EPBD obligations.
seo.chargesTitle: Co-ownership charges distribution: rules and best practices
seo.chargesContent:
Common charges distribution in Luxembourg co-ownership follows precise rules:

  • General charges (art. 6, law 1975): distributed according to co-ownership shares proportional to the relative value of each private lot.
  • Special charges: certain charges may be distributed by utility (elevator by floor, heating by area).
  • Reserve fund: building a reserve fund for major works is recommended (minimum 5% of annual budget).
  • Transparency: the syndic must present detailed annual accounts and the forecast budget at the GA.
seo.renovationTitle: Energy renovation in co-ownership: obligations and subsidies
seo.renovationContent:
Enter VAT-inclusive quotes and already confirmed grants, all initially zero. No amount is inferred automatically from the EPC class. Results assume grants are immediately available and exclude financing. The target class must be assessed by an energy adviser.

For residential buildings, the EPBD sets a national average-consumption trajectory. An EPC letter alone does not establish an individual 2030 or 2033 deadline. Applicable national rules must be checked for the building.

Allocation by ownership shares is a budgeting assumption. Each beneficiary's eligibility and the building's allocation rules must be checked; grants are not automatically transferable between units.
seo.reglementationContent:
The legal framework applicable to co-ownerships in Luxembourg includes:

  • Law of 16 May 1975: co-ownership status for buildings — defines rules, rights and obligations of co-owners, the role of the syndic.
  • Grand-ducal regulation of 13 June 1975: implementing measures of the 1975 law.
  • Law of 21 September 2006: residential lease — regulates rents and recoverable charges.
  • Grand-ducal regulation of 5 May 2023: PRIMe House financial aids for energy renovation.
  • EPBD Directive 2024/1275: energy performance of buildings — renovation deadlines.
seo.faq1A: Shares are calculated proportionally to the relative value of each private lot compared to the total building value. This value considers the area, location (floor, exposure), and consistency of the lot. They are set in the co-ownership regulations and can only be modified by unanimous vote.
seo.faq2Q: What majorities are needed to vote on energy renovation works?
seo.faq2A: Routine maintenance works can be voted by simple majority (50% + 1 of shares). Improvement works (including deep energy renovation) require a qualified majority of 2/3 of represented shares. Works modifying the building's purpose require unanimity.
seo.faq3Q: How to finance the energy renovation of a co-ownership in Luxembourg?
seo.faq3A: Enter VAT-inclusive quotes and already confirmed grants, all initially zero. No amount is inferred automatically from the EPC class. Results assume grants are immediately available and exclude financing. The target class must be assessed by an energy adviser.
seo.faq4Q: What are the syndic's obligations regarding energy?
seo.faq4A: For residential buildings, the EPBD sets a national average-consumption trajectory. An EPC letter alone does not establish an individual 2030 or 2033 deadline. Applicable national rules must be checked for the building.

seo.usaliContent: Enter payroll, including employer contributions, once in its dedicated categories; exclude it from other expenses. Document every category, including absent ones with zero. Non-operating expenses may include rent, property insurance and property taxes; exclude interest, income taxes, depreciation, amortisation and FF&E reserve. Use a consistent VAT basis. GOP = departmental profit − general expenses. EBITDA = GOP − management fees + non-operating income − non-operating expenses. The reserve is deducted afterwards. This simplified statement is not USALI certification, a benchmark or net profit after financing and income tax.
seo.faq1q: What does the Hospitality Solutions hub cover?

seo.faq2q: Is the PMS compliant with Luxembourg tax rules?
seo.faq2a: Check reservations, charges, rates and supporting documents before producing an invoice or report. Stored data alone does not establish tax or accounting validity. The rate depends on the service and VAT Act schedules. F&B does not determine one universal rate. Check each line and any local tax against applicable sources.

seo.faq4q: What is the difference between GOP, EBITDA and net income?
seo.faq4a: GOP = departmental profit − general expenses. EBITDA = GOP − management fees + non-operating income − non-operating expenses. The reserve is deducted afterwards. This simplified statement is not USALI certification, a benchmark or net profit after financing and income tax.

seo.faq6a: Ask the bank which scope, valuation date, methods and qualifications it requires for your case. No universal loan threshold or bank acceptance is guaranteed here. A SHA-256 hash checks file integrity; by itself it is neither an electronic signature nor a professional valuation.

seo.contextTitle: A guided journey for confident decisions
seo.contextContent: Buying in Luxembourg means juggling four questions: how much is the property worth, what are the acquisition fees, which state aids apply, and — if you plan to rent it out — what is the legal rent cap under the 5% rule. Our journey chains these four steps and automatically reuses the information you have already entered.
seo.etapesContent: 1. Estimation: price per sqm by municipality/neighbourhood, adjusted for condition, floor, outdoor, parking and energy class. 2. Acquisition fees: registration duties, Bëllegen Akt credit, 3% VAT on new primary residence, notary fees, mortgage registration. 3. Aids: the 5 layers (state, energy retrofit, private, communal, heritage). 4. 5% rule: legal rent cap if you plan to rent the property.
seo.avantagesTitle: Why a journey rather than four separate tools
seo.avantagesContent: Your negotiated price flows automatically into fees and aids. Ticking primary residence or new construction in step 2 changes the aid thresholds in step 3. The final recap computes the estimated net cost (price + fees − cash aids) so you immediately know the total capital to mobilise.
seo.limitesTitle: What the journey does not replace
seo.limitesContent: This journey provides an indicative estimate based on public data from Observatoire de l'Habitat, STATEC and Luxembourg tax scales. It does not replace a personalised loan simulation from a bank, nor a formal TEGOVA EVS 2025 valuation report for a binding transaction.
seo.faq1q: Do I need an account to use the journey?
seo.faq1a: No. The journey runs entirely in your browser. No data is sent to our servers unless you explicitly save your scenario in a logged-in account.
seo.faq2q: Does the estimation account for energy class?
seo.faq2a: Yes. Energy class adjusts the per-sqm price using hedonic coefficients observed on the Luxembourg market: a bonus for A/B, a progressive discount from class E.
seo.faq3q: Which aids are computed?
seo.faq3a: All 5 layers: state acquisition aids (Bëllegen Akt, 3% VAT relief), energy renovation (Klimabonus, Klimaprêt), private aids (housing savings premium), communal aids (variable by municipality) and heritage aids (listed properties).
seo.faq4q: Does the 5% rule apply if I live in the property myself?
seo.faq4a: No. The legal cap applies only to rented properties. If you buy for yourself, skip step 4 — it is only relevant if you plan to rent the property later.

seo.klimabonusContent: The energy class alone does not determine Klimabonus entitlement. Check the building, works, dates and applicable prior approval.
seo.rendementContent: Gross yield divides annual rent by the purchase price. The legal rent ceiling uses a different basis: revalued and depreciated invested capital. It therefore does not set a maximum gross yield of 5% of the purchase price.

seo.methodContent: RevPAR (Revenue per Available Room) = ADR × occupancy rate. Multiplied by 365 × number of rooms, it gives annual room revenue. Add F&B and other department revenue to get total revenue. Subtract operating charges (staff, energy, other opex) for GOP, then FF&E reserve (4%) for stabilised EBITDA. DCF value = EBITDA / capitalisation rate.
seo.ratiosContent: Budget (1-2★): staff 28-32%, energy 7-9%, other opex 22-26%, GOP 30-40%. Midscale (3★): staff 30-34%, GOP 28-35%. Upscale (4★): staff 32-36%, GOP 25-32%. Luxury (5★): staff 35-40%, GOP 20-28%. Ranges sourced from PKF Hotel Experts and STR Global, calibrated on the European market.
seo.capRateTitle: Capitalisation rate: the most sensitive variable
seo.capRateContent: A cap rate of 7% instead of 8% mechanically raises DCF value by 14%. Observed rates in Europe 2025: luxury 4.5-6% (Paris, Milan, Zurich), upscale 6-7.5%, midscale 7-9%, budget 8-11%. For a secondary LU/BE hotel, 7.5-9% is the prudent compromise.
seo.faq1q: What does 'stabilised EBITDA' mean?
seo.faq1a: EBITDA in cruising year post-ramp-up, after 3-5 years of operation from acquisition or repositioning. Not the EBITDA of year N-1 if abnormal (covid, works, major local event).
seo.faq2q: Why 4% FF&E reserve?
seo.faq2a: Furniture, Fixtures & Equipment: gradual replacement of furniture and equipment. 4% is the USALI 11th ed. standard. A luxury hotel may justify 5-6%, an economy motel holding at 3%.
seo.faq3q: Should I use DCF or price-per-key?
seo.faq3a: Both. The DCF approach reflects the unique economic performance of the asset. The price-per-key multiple anchors on market prices. The arithmetic mean typically sets the retained range; a gap > 30% signals an atypical asset.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions

seo.definitionTitle: DSCR: the ratio the bank looks at first
seo.definitionContent: DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) = EBITDA / (principal + annual interest). A commercial bank typically requires DSCR ≥ 1.30 on a hotel loan. SBA 7(a) US: 1.25. LBO/mezzanine: 1.50. Below 1.00, the hotel does not cover its payments — the file is rejected.
seo.stressTitle: Stress tests: real robustness of the file
seo.stressContent: A central DSCR at 1.40 may hide fragility. Three stress tests to verify: occupancy −10 pts (covid effect), ADR −10% (competitive or recession pressure), combined double shock (−25% RevPAR). If DSCR falls below 1.00 under double shock, the file is risky for the bank.
seo.ltvContent: Loan-to-Value = debt / asset value. In LU/BE hospitality, banks finance 65-75% (vs 80% in residential). The 25-35% equity can be complemented by a mezzanine loan (cost 8-12%), seller credit (negotiated with the seller) or a regional commercial fund.
seo.faq1q: Why stricter DSCR in hospitality?
seo.faq1a: Higher revenue volatility than in residential rental. A hotel depends on occupancy and ADR, both sensitive to the economic cycle. A DSCR of 1.30 provides a 23% safety margin before default — about one bad quarter.
seo.faq2q: What if DSCR is borderline (1.10-1.25)?
seo.faq2a: Three levers: increase equity (lower monthly payment), extend duration (20 → 25 years), negotiate lower rate. Caution: extending duration raises total credit cost. Additional equity remains the cleanest solution.
seo.faq3q: How to estimate EBITDA if the hotel is new?
seo.faq3a: Use the Operation USALI tool to build a 5-year P&L forecast with ramp-up (lower year 1 occupancy, progressive over 3 years). Retain the years 3-5 average as stabilised EBITDA for DSCR.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions

seo.usaliContent: The Uniform System of Accounts for the Lodging Industry, published by AHLA, has standardised hotel operating accounts globally since 1926. The 11th edition (2014) remains the worldwide reference. Structure: revenue by department (Rooms, F&B, Other), charges by department, undistributed charges (A&G, marketing, maintenance, energy), GOP, fixed charges, EBITDA.
seo.gopContent: GOP (Gross Operating Profit) is the key operator performance line. Typical GOP margins: budget 30-40%, midscale 28-35%, upscale 25-32%, luxury 20-28%. A GOP below range signals operational inefficiency (over-staffing, uncontrolled energy, high food cost). The tool automatically compares your projection to the chosen category.
seo.ffeTitle: FF&E reserve: 4% required in bank valuation
seo.ffeContent: Furniture, Fixtures & Equipment: reserve for replacing furniture, linen, TV, IT, small equipment. 4% of total revenue is the standard required by banks and USALI for any valuation. A hotel claiming EBITDA = GOP without FF&E deduction overstates its result by about 15-25%.
seo.faq1q: Is the forecast conservative or optimistic?
seo.faq1a: The tool applies average USALI ratios for the chosen category. For a prudent forecast required by a bank, increase staff by 2-3 points and lower ADR by 5%. For an aggressive investor business plan, the reverse.
seo.faq2q: How to project ramp-up of a new hotel?
seo.faq2a: Year 1: 50-55% occupancy. Year 2: 60-65%. Year 3-5: 65-75% (stabilised). ADR grows 2-3%/year via inflation + repositioning. The tool manages this curve via 'ADR growth' and 'occupancy progression' parameters.
seo.faq3q: F&B: profitable revenue or cost?
seo.faq3a: Strongly category-dependent. Budget: F&B often loss-making (breakfast included), contributes via differentiation. Midscale: F&B at break-even. Upscale/Luxury: F&B can contribute 15-25% of total GOP if the restaurant attracts clients beyond hotel guests.

seo.klimabonusContent: A hotel does not automatically qualify for residential Klimabonus. Verify building use, beneficiary business, eligible expenditure, application date and cumulation rules. Zero included aid means no amount is counted in this scenario, not an ineligibility decision.
seo.tertiaireContent: A hotel does not automatically qualify for residential Klimabonus. Verify building use, beneficiary business, eligible expenditure, application date and cumulation rules. Zero included aid means no amount is counted in this scenario, not an ineligibility decision.
seo.roiTitle: ROI: energy savings + RevPAR gain via label
seo.roiContent: Scenario assumptions, with no validation of cost or technical performance. Entered grants are assumed immediately available and allocated proportionally to costs; no Klimabonus rate is awarded. Commercial gains are multiplied by the entered margin, then added to energy savings net of maintenance. Ten-year NPV at 4%, constant year-end flows, excluding debt, tax, recoverable VAT, future replacements and residual value. Use the detailed scenario for delayed grants or financing.
seo.faq1q: Can Klimabonus be combined with other aids?
seo.faq1a: A hotel does not automatically qualify for residential Klimabonus. Verify building use, beneficiary business, eligible expenditure, application date and cumulation rules. Zero included aid means no amount is counted in this scenario, not an ineligibility decision.
seo.faq2q: Which retrofit item offers the best ROI?
seo.faq2a: Scenario assumptions, with no validation of cost or technical performance. Entered grants are assumed immediately available and allocated proportionally to costs; no Klimabonus rate is awarded. Commercial gains are multiplied by the entered margin, then added to energy savings net of maintenance. Ten-year NPV at 4%, constant year-end flows, excluding debt, tax, recoverable VAT, future replacements and residual value. Use the detailed scenario for delayed grants or financing.
seo.faq3q: Does an eco-label actually raise ADR?
seo.faq3a: Entered commercial assumption, 0% by default. A label guarantees no RevPAR uplift.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions

seo.indicesTitle: MPI, ARI, RGI: the three fair-share indices
seo.indicesContent: MPI (Market Penetration Index) = hotel occupancy / compset occupancy × 100. Measures your volume performance. ARI (Average Rate Index) = hotel ADR / compset ADR × 100. Measures your pricing. RGI (Revenue Generation Index) = MPI × ARI / 100 ≈ hotel RevPAR / compset RevPAR × 100. The reference index for overall positioning.
seo.compsetContent: A compset (competitive set) typically groups 4-7 hotels of the same geographic segment and category. Criteria: same area (city, tourist district), same star category, same positioning (business vs leisure), comparable size. Data come from STR subscriptions or direct exchange between hoteliers (common in Luxembourg via Hotrec LU).
seo.fairShareTitle: Interpretation: fair share, price problem, commercial problem
seo.fairShareContent: RGI ≈ 100: fair share reached, market-level performance. RGI < 95 with low MPI and good ARI: distribution/commercial problem (visibility, channels, reputation). RGI < 95 with good MPI and low ARI: pricing problem (under-pricing to fill). RGI > 105: over-performance — watch the market ceiling, lever for rate increase.
seo.faq1q: Where to find compset data without STR subscription?
seo.faq1a: STR Global costs €5-20k/year depending on market. Free alternatives: Hotrec LU quarterly sharing, OTA dashboards (Booking, Expedia), bilateral agreements between local hoteliers. Chambers of commerce sometimes provide aggregated data by canton.
seo.faq2q: Recommended analysis frequency?
seo.faq2a: Monthly for a cruising hotel. Weekly in high season or during repositioning phase. Revenue managers also use daily tracking on 14-day rolling windows during critical periods (trade shows, event weekends).
seo.faq3q: My RGI is good but GOP is bad — why?
seo.faq3a: RGI measures top-line performance (revenue vs market). GOP measures operational profitability. A hotel can have excellent RGI and weak GOP if it over-staffs, overpays for energy or keeps disproportionate fixed charges. Use the Operation USALI tool to identify the problem item.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions

seo.visaTitle: The E-2 visa: an immigration tool via investment
seo.visaContent: The E-2 (Treaty Investor) visa allows citizens of treaty countries with the United States (incl. Luxembourg, France, Belgium) to obtain an indefinitely renewable work visa via substantial investment in an active American business. Acquiring a hotel or motel is a preferred route: tangible asset, job creation, active not passive operation.
seo.criteresContent: 1. Substantiality: invested capital vs total project cost (typically 50-100% if project < $500k, decreasing for larger projects). 2. At-risk: funds actually committed (escrow, signed contracts). 3. Marginality: income above US family minimum vital. 4. Real & operating: active hotel, not passive holding. 5. Job creation: US jobs created or maintained (excluding investor and family).
seo.limitContent: This tool computes an indicative score on the 5 key criteria. It does not replace consulting an E-2-specialised US immigration lawyer. Subjective elements (quality of business plan, investor professional history, tax compliance, target hotel due diligence) are not considered and remain decisive for actual visa grant.
seo.faq1q: What minimum capital for a hotel E-2 visa?
seo.faq1a: No official USCIS threshold. In practice, $100-200k is considered a floor. For a hotel/motel, typical range is $300-800k equity for an $800k-$2M project, with creation of 4-10 US jobs.
seo.faq2q: Duration and renewal of E-2 visa?
seo.faq2a: Initial visa 2-5 years depending on country (5 years for LU/FR/BE). Indefinitely renewable as long as criteria (active business, maintained jobs, committed funds) are met. Each renewal costs $200-400 + legal fees.
seo.faq3q: Can children and spouse work or study?
seo.faq3a: Spouse: can apply for a US work permit (EAD) without sector restriction. Children: can study in any US public or private school (K-12, university). At 21, children lose derived status — they must change visa.

seo.contextContent: Commercial leases in Luxembourg are governed by the law of 3 February 2018 and the Civil Code. Unlike residential leases, the rent is freely agreed at signing — the 5% rule capping rent does not apply. Instead, the 9-year minimum duration and the right to renewal provide strong tenant protection.
seo.indexationContent: Luxembourg has no specific commercial-lease index (no French ILC/ILAT equivalent). Parties usually reference the Consumer Price Index (CPI) published by STATEC. Clauses often cap indexation at 15-25% of the initial rent to limit drifts in high-inflation periods.
seo.dureeContent: The 3 February 2018 law sets a 9-year minimum for commercial leases. The tenant may terminate at each triennial period (3, 6, 9 years) with 6-month notice. Absent 6-month notice before term, the lease renews tacitly.
seo.faq1q: Does the 5% rule apply to commerce?
seo.faq1a: No. The 5% rule (legal rent cap based on reassessed invested capital) is specific to residential leases. For commercial leases, the initial rent is freely negotiated between landlord and tenant.
seo.faq2q: How is commercial rent indexed in LU?
seo.faq2a: Through the Consumer Price Index (CPI) published by STATEC, per the formula negotiated in the lease. Usual formula: indexed rent = initial rent × (CPI year N / CPI year of signature), often capped at +15% or +20% of the initial rent.
seo.faq3q: What is the minimum duration?
seo.faq3a: 9 years (law of 3 February 2018). Tenant may exit at each triennial period with 6-month notice. Landlord may only terminate at the 9-year term for personal use or major works, otherwise an eviction indemnity is owed.
seo.faq4q: What is the « pas-de-porte »?
seo.faq4a: A sum paid by the incoming tenant to the landlord in exchange for the right to occupy. May equal several months or years of rent. Not refundable and distinct from the security deposit (usually 3-12 months).

hotelForecast.subtitle: Indicative hotel projection: occupancy, ADR and RevPAR from consecutive recorded days. Variation scenarios are selected by the user, with no associated probability.
hotelForecast.seedConfirm: Generate 120 days of synthetic data to test the forecast? (marked 'forecast_seed', deletable)
hotelForecast.csvFormat: CSV: date,occupancy,adr, one row per day. YYYY-MM-DD dates; occupancy 0.75 or 75% (1=100%, 1%=0.01; percentages require the % sign). Decimal commas with semicolon delimiter. Non-negative ADR. Invalid files are rejected in full. Existing dates are replaced by imported rows.
hotelForecast.noCsvRows: No valid rows detected in the CSV.
hotelForecast.minDataWarning: At least 14 unique consecutive days are required, with no missing values for the selected metric, and a variation between 0 and 100%. Dates must be valid and not in the future. RevPAR requires occupancy and ADR for every day.
hotelForecast.methodology: Additive weekly Holt-Winters, 7-day period and fixed α=0.3, β=0.1, γ=0.3. Forecast occupancy is bounded to 0–100%, ADR to zero minimum. RevPAR is recalculated as occupancy × ADR, with its forecast combining both projected series. Displayed averages are simple daily means, not ratios weighted by rooms sold or available. The band only applies the selected variation, bounded by metric: no confidence interval or independent backtest. Shocks, future events and capacity changes are not modeled. Demonstration data are excluded.
hotelForecast.excludedDemo: Older rows marked as demonstration are excluded from calculations. They remain visible in the history and are not deleted.

transparencePage.pageDescription: Methodology, coefficients, data sources and back-test results. This page is public: any user can verify the quality and limitations of our model.
transparencePage.methodoP1: The model combines a reference price per m² (by municipality or neighbourhood, from the Observatoire de l'Habitat via data.public.lu) with multiplicative adjustments reflecting the property's intrinsic characteristics. This is not an AVM (Automated Valuation Model) in the banking sense — it does not have the completeness of notarial deeds.
transparencePage.methodoP2: Each adjustment is an additive percentage (positive or negative) applied to the base price. The coefficients come from the Observatoire de l'Habitat, Spuerkeess analyses and professional valuation practice in Luxembourg.
transparencePage.srcObservatoireData: Price/m² per municipality, Lux-City neighbourhoods, hedonic model
transparencePage.srcSpuerkeessData: Energy class impact on sale price
transparencePage.srcPubliciteFonciereData: Transaction volume per municipality (number of deeds)
transparencePage.coeffDesc: Each coefficient is a percentage applied to the reference price per m². The confidence level reflects the statistical robustness of the source.
transparencePage.backtestDesc: Reference prices for these examples are defined in the model using market ranges. These are not verified transactions or an independent validation. The indicators above describe only these examples and do not measure accuracy on actual sales.
transparencePage.limite1: Observatory data is aggregated by municipality — sub-municipal granularity (street, subdivision) is not captured.
transparencePage.limite2: Atypical properties (castles, investment buildings, architect-designed houses) are not covered by this model.
transparencePage.limite3: Micro-market effects (view, nuisances, orientation) are not modelled due to lack of structured data.
transparencePage.limite4: Reference prices reflect T-4 deeds; in a very dynamic market, a 3-6 month lag may exist.
transparencePage.limite5: This model does not replace a TEGOVA/RICS expert valuation with physical visit — it provides a quick order of magnitude.
transparencePage.engagementText: this page will be updated with each recalibration (quarterly, aligned with Observatory publications). Professional users (banks, agencies) can verify the model's reliability before integrating it into their workflow.

fraisNotaire.metaDescription: Separate amounts paid to the State, the notary’s remuneration, VAT and costs specific to the transaction.
fraisNotaire.subtitle: Separate amounts paid to the State, the notary’s remuneration, VAT and costs specific to the transaction.
essentiel: For an ordinary purchase for consideration, registration duty is 6% and transcription duty is 1%, totalling 7%. These are not the notary’s fees. Exemptions, special tax bases and possible surcharges must be checked for the deed.

The personal credit is for purchases meeting the own-occupation conditions, including occupation for at least two years. The notary submits the application. Check each buyer’s remaining balance: EUR 40,000 is the ceiling confirmed by the official sources consulted, not a fresh credit for every purchase.
Private sale: tariff 7 of the notarial regulation, minimum €99.16 excluding VAT, plus 17% VAT. Copies, disbursements, travel and exceptional work must be added from the notary’s statement.
Ordinary non-exempt mortgage loan: 0.24% of principal, 0.05% of the secured amount, tariff 5 and VAT. Exemptions, mortgage discharge, copies and bank fees are not calculated.

faq.a: For an off-plan purchase, have the deed distinguish land, completed works and works still to be performed: duties are not always limited to land alone. The 3% VAT rate on eligible new construction requires, in particular, use as the owner’s principal home and an available tax benefit, capped at EUR 50,000 per dwelling. faq.q: What is the Bëllegen Akt and how do I get it?

faq.q: Which tariff schedule applies?

Schedule 7 applies to a private sale through successive bands: add the portions rather than applying the marginal rate to the entire price. The table shows cumulative assessment thresholds. Private sale: tariff 7 of the notarial regulation, minimum €99.16 excluding VAT, plus 17% VAT. Copies, disbursements, travel and exceptional work must be added from the notary’s statement.

faq.q: How should you prepare the breakdown with the notary?
faq.a: Provide the draft deed, ownership shares, personal credit balances, intended use and, where relevant, the loan principal and secured ancillary amounts. Request an itemised call for funds and the costs still to be added.

faq.q: Are notary fees tax-deductible in Luxembourg?
faq.a: For a privately held rental property, the tax administration distinguishes acquisition costs, included in the cost basis and depreciable for the building share, from financing costs, including the mortgage obligation deed, deductible under the expense rules. Land is not depreciable. Do not apply this rule wholesale to your own home: establish the treatment and tax year of each item.

regle5Pourcent.title: Luxembourg 5 % rent rule: calculation and 2026 reform
regle5Pourcent.metaDescription: The annual rent cap excluding charges is 5% of revalued invested capital after net depreciation. It is neither 5% of current market value nor a guaranteed yield. Recoverable charges are separate.
regle5Pourcent.subtitle: How Luxembourg's statutory rent cap works, how to compute it, and the impact of the upcoming reform.
essentiel: Annual rent ≤ 5% of revalued invested capital (Art. 3 of the 2006 law). The landlord cannot demand more, even by agreement.
Invested capital = purchase price + deed costs + durable improvement works (excluding routine maintenance and decoration).
Revaluation via the STATEC coefficient for the purchase year (1.52 for 2025, 1.77 for 2022, 2.07 for 2015).
2%/year wear-and-tear discount on the construction share (Art. 5 RGD 2015).
Reform under way (bill 8184): cap lowered to 3.5% for new leases, expected entry into force 2026.
regle5Pourcent.section1P1: Article 3 of the modified law of 21 September 2006 on residential leases sets the maximum annual rent at 5% of the revalued capital invested in the rented property. It is an imperative cap: any clause providing a higher rent is void, and the tenant can obtain a retroactive rent reduction before the municipal Rent Commission or the justice of the peace.
regle5Pourcent.section1P2: The mechanism seeks a balance between a reasonable return for the landlord (5% gross/year) and tenant protection. The rule applies to rent excluding charges. Service charges (water, heating, common area maintenance, elevator) are billed separately at actual cost, within the recoverable charges set by the Grand Ducal Regulation of 16 June 2015.
regle5Pourcent.callout1Title: The cap excludes charges and furnished
regle5Pourcent.callout1Body: Service charges sit on top of the legal cap, on actual cost basis. For furnished accommodation, a supplement may apply for the furniture (typically 0.5 to 1% extra depending on inventory). Company housing and leases concluded before 2007 are also excluded from the strict 5% cap.
regle5Pourcent.section2P1: Invested capital comprises: the property's purchase price (land + construction), deed costs (duties, emoluments, mortgage), and subsequent durable improvement expenses (extensions, transformation, major energy renovation). Excluded are routine maintenance, decoration, furniture, and finance costs.
regle5Pourcent.section2P2: Capital is revalued at the date of rent setting using the revaluation coefficient of the investment year, published by STATEC. Key 2026 coefficients: 1.48 (2026), 1.52 (2025), 1.57 (2024), 1.64 (2023), 1.77 (2022), 2.07 (2015), 2.33 (2010). A 2%/year wear-and-tear discount applies to the construction share (RGD 16.06.2015).
regle5Pourcent.callout2Body: Only durable expenses that increase the property's value enter invested capital: insulation, boiler replacement, electrical upgrade, extensions. Pure conservation works (paint, façade refresh, joints) do not count. If unsure, request an opinion from the Rent Commission before setting the new rent.
regle5Pourcent.section3P1: Full formula: Max annual rent = (revalued invested capital − construction wear-and-tear discount) × 5%. Max monthly rent = max annual rent / 12. Example: apartment bought €400,000 in 2015 (€30,000 in costs), no works. 2015 coefficient = 2.07. Revalued capital = €430,000 × 2.07 = €890,100. Wear-and-tear 11 years × 2% = 22% (on the ~70% construction share). Capital after wear-and-tear ≈ €753,700. Max annual rent = 5% × €753,700 = €37,685/year, i.e., ~€3,140/month.
regle5Pourcent.section3P2: In case of dispute, tenant or landlord can refer to the municipal Rent Commission (free procedure, Art. 7 of the 2006 law). The Commission issues an opinion based on the documents: acquisition deed, works invoices, quotes, STATEC indices. If the opinion is ignored, the matter can go before the justice of the peace, who can impose retroactive reduction and refund of overpayments.
regle5Pourcent.section4Intro: Maximum monthly rent for a typical apartment bought €400,000 + €30,000 in costs (€430,000 total capital). Construction share is estimated at 70% of the price.

table.footnote: Indicative computation after 2%/year wear-and-tear on the construction share (70% of price). Reform 8184: with a 3.5% cap, these rents would drop by about 30%.

regle5Pourcent.callout3Body: Property bought €500,000 + €35,000 costs in 2018, 6 years of holding. 2018 coefficient ≈ 1.99. Revalued capital = €535,000 × 1.99 = €1,064,650. Wear-and-tear = 12% on 70% = 8.4%. Net capital ≈ €974,800. Max annual rent = 5% × €974,800 = €48,740. Max monthly rent ≈ €4,060. With the proposed 3.5% reform, the cap would drop to about €2,845/month.

faq.q: How to calculate the maximum rent in Luxembourg?
faq.a: Multiply invested capital (purchase price + deed costs + improvement works) by the STATEC coefficient of the investment year. Apply the 2%/year wear-and-tear discount on the construction share. Multiply the result by 5% to get the max annual rent, then divide by 12 for monthly.

faq.q: Will the 5% rule change in Luxembourg?
faq.a: Bill 8184 plans to lower the cap from 5% to 3.5% for new leases, aiming to better protect tenants against rising prices. The text is in parliamentary discussion and could enter into force during 2026. Existing leases would not be retroactively affected.

faq.q: What exactly is included in invested capital?
faq.a: The purchase price of land and construction, deed costs (duties, emoluments, mortgage), and durable improvement expenses (extensions, transformation, major energy renovation). Routine maintenance, decoration and furniture are excluded.

faq.q: How does the 2% wear-and-tear discount work?
faq.a: The construction share (excluding land, typically 60-75% of price depending on the municipality) is discounted by 2% per year elapsed since purchase or last structural works. The discount cumulates up to a floor (typically 30% of the initial value).

faq.q: Are service charges included in the 5% cap?
faq.a: No. Charges (water, heating, common maintenance, elevator) are billed on top of the capped rent, on an actual cost basis and limitatively listed in the Grand Ducal Regulation of 16 June 2015 (waste tax, common utilities, etc.). The landlord cannot pass on major works or a margin.

faq.q: What if my rent exceeds the legal cap?
faq.a: Refer free of charge to your municipality's Rent Commission with the landlord's acquisition deed (request it), your lease and works invoices. The Commission issues an opinion; if the landlord refuses to comply, you can go before the justice of the peace, who can order a retroactive reduction and refund of overpayments.

plusValue.title: Luxembourg real estate capital gains: 2026 tax rules (LIR)
plusValue.metaDescription: In 2026, private sales held for no more than five years are speculative; longer holdings may qualify for half the overall tax rate. In 2025, the two-year threshold and quarter overall rate apply through 30 June, and from 1 July to 30 September if the preliminary agreement was registered with AED by 30 June. Exact dates matter.
plusValue.subtitle: Understand the taxation of a real estate capital gain by holding period, property use and applicable tax regime.
essentiel: Holding < 2 years = speculation profit: progressive income tax, up to about 45.78% with employment fund contribution.
Holding ≥ 2 years = transfer profit: one quarter of the global tax rate (typical effective 10 to 11%).
Acquisition price is revalued via the STATEC coefficient (1.52 for a 2025 purchase, 1.48 for 2026).
Decennial allowance: €50,000 per person, €100,000 for a jointly taxed couple.
Primary residence personally and continuously occupied: full exemption possible.
plusValue.section1P1: Luxembourg tax law distinguishes two regimes by holding period. If resale occurs within two years of acquisition, the gain is a speculation profit (Art. 99bis LIR): it is fully added to that year's taxable income and taxed at the progressive income tax rate (marginal up to 42% + 7 or 9% employment fund contribution, max effective around 45.78%).
plusValue.section1P2: Beyond two years' holding, the gain becomes a transfer profit (Art. 99ter LIR) under a much more favourable regime: only one quarter of the overall tax rate applies under article 102bis paragraph 1 LIR. For a taxpayer in the 42% marginal bracket, the effective rate on the gain falls to about 10.5%, after allowance.
plusValue.callout1Body: The holding period runs from the date of the authentic acquisition deed to the date of the disposal deed. The sale compromis does not stop the clock. For a property received by gift or inheritance, the period starts from the original acquisition date by the donor or deceased (Art. 99bis para. 3 LIR).
plusValue.section2P1: The gross gain is the difference between the disposal price (less selling costs such as agency commission) and the acquisition price increased by deed costs (duties, emoluments, mortgage) and durable improvement expenses (extensions, structural works, major energy renovation). Routine maintenance is not deductible.
plusValue.section2P2: For the transfer regime (≥ 2 years), the acquisition price and costs are revalued using the revaluation coefficient published annually by STATEC (Art. 102 LIR). For 2026, key coefficients are: 2.33 (2010 purchase), 2.07 (2015), 1.77 (2022), 1.52 (2025). A property bought for €400,000 in 2015 has a revalued price of about €828,000. The gross gain is then reduced by the decennial allowance and taxed at one quarter of the global rate.
plusValue.section3P1: The decennial allowance under article 130 paragraph 4 LIR removes €50,000 from the taxable gain per person (€100,000 for a jointly taxed couple). It is rechargeable every ten years, allowing planning of disposals after reconstitution. The primary residence effectively and continuously occupied for the five years preceding disposal is fully exempt (Art. 102bis para. 3 LIR), with no price cap.
plusValue.section3P2: A tax deferral (reinvestment) is possible if sale proceeds are reinvested into a new owner-occupied primary residence within two years (Art. 102bis para. 2 LIR). For land, specific regimes exist (deferral on gift to a descendant). Gratuitous transfers (gift, inheritance) do not trigger taxation for the donor, but the beneficiary takes over the historical acquisition price for computing their own future gain.
plusValue.callout2Body: The decennial allowance is reconstituted in ten-year tranches from the last use. An investor planning multiple disposals can space them out to benefit from a fresh allowance each tranche — particularly attractive for couples (€100,000 per tranche).
plusValue.section4Intro: Combined effects of the revaluation coefficient, the decennial allowance and the quarter of the global rate for a property bought in 2015 and sold in 2026 (purchase €400,000, deed costs €30,000, sale €700,000, taxpayer at 42% marginal global rate).

faq.q: What is the capital gains tax rate on real estate in Luxembourg?
faq.a: Within 2 years (speculation), progressive income tax up to about 45.78% effective. Beyond 2 years (transfer), one quarter of the global rate, typically 10 to 11% depending on bracket, after the decennial allowance.

faq.q: Is the sale of my primary residence taxable?
faq.a: No, provided you have effectively and continuously occupied it as your primary residence for the 5 years preceding the disposal. The gain is fully exempt (Art. 102bis para. 3 LIR), with no sale price cap.

faq.q: How does the decennial allowance work?
faq.a: Every taxpayer is granted €50,000 (€100,000 for a jointly taxed couple) off the taxable gain, rechargeable every ten years. If you dispose of two properties in the same decade, the allowance applies only once.

faq.q: How is the revaluation coefficient calculated?
faq.a: It is published annually by STATEC under article 102 LIR and reflects the construction price index since the acquisition year. For 2026: 2.33 (2010 purchase), 2.07 (2015), 1.77 (2022), 1.52 (2025), 1.48 (2026).

faq.q: Are acquisition costs included in the calculation?
faq.a: Yes. Registration duties, notary emoluments, mortgage costs of the acquisition deed and durable improvement expenses (extensions, major renovation, major energy upgrades) are added to the purchase price before revaluation. Routine maintenance and decoration are not deductible.

faq.q: What about gifts or inheritance?
faq.a: A gift or inheritance does not trigger capital gains tax for the donor or deceased (Art. 99bis para. 4 LIR). The beneficiary takes over the historical acquisition price and original acquisition date when computing their own future gain, which can lead to significant latent gains.

essentiel: Legal framework: modified law of 21 September 2006 on residential tenancy, complemented by the Civil Code and the Grand Ducal Regulation of 16 June 2015 on charges.
Default duration: indefinite. Tenant notice 3 months, landlord notice 6 months and only for legitimate reason (personal need, serious breach, works).
Rent capped at 5% per year of revalued invested capital (Art. 3 of the 2006 law). See the dedicated guide on the 5% rule.
Rental deposit: maximum 3 months' rent excluding charges, on a blocked account in the tenant's name. Interest belongs to the tenant.
Free pre-judicial remedy: municipal Rent Commission before any court action.
bailHabitation.section1P1: Residential leases in Luxembourg are framed by the modified law of 21 September 2006, which applies to any rental of a dwelling used as a primary residence (article 1). Excluded: short-term furnished holiday rentals, agricultural leases and commercial leases (governed by other laws). The contract must be in writing; without writing, the law still recognises the lease as soon as there is payment and occupation, but with a heavier burden of proof.
bailHabitation.section1P2: The lease is concluded for an indefinite duration by default. Fixed-term leases are possible but, at expiry, automatically convert into indefinite leases if the tenant remains in occupation without the landlord's opposition (tacit renewal). The contract must mention the parties, dwelling description, rent excluding charges, charge amount and calculation basis, deposit amount and entry date.
bailHabitation.callout1Body: Void clauses include: any deposit greater than 3 months' rent, any unlimited solidarity of a co-tenant after their departure, any termination penalty outside the legal notice, and any clause exempting the landlord from delivering a decent dwelling (Art. 1719 Civil Code).
bailHabitation.section2P1: The initial rent is free but cannot exceed 5% of revalued invested capital (Art. 3 of the 2006 law). Rent can only be revised once every two years, and only upwards in line with the STATEC consumer price index, or if improvement works justify a re-evaluation of the invested capital. Revision must be notified by registered letter with one month's notice.
bailHabitation.section2P2: The deposit is limited to 3 months' rent excluding charges (Art. 5 of the 2006 law). It must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name at a Luxembourg bank; interest earned belongs to the tenant. Restitution must occur within a reasonable time after the lease ends (typically 1 to 3 months), minus any damages noted at the exit inventory. A State rental guarantee is available for eligible tenants via the Ministry of Housing.
bailHabitation.section3P1: The landlord must deliver the dwelling in good condition (Art. 1719 Civil Code), guarantee peaceful enjoyment, carry out major repairs (roof, facade, structure, major electrical compliance) and produce joint entry and exit inventories. The landlord may only recover from the tenant the charges exhaustively listed in the Grand Ducal Regulation of 16 June 2015: water/electricity/gas of common areas, collective heating, common area maintenance, elevator, municipal waste tax, building liability insurance.
bailHabitation.section3P2: The tenant must pay rent on time, use the dwelling responsibly, perform minor tenant repairs (seals, light bulbs, small fixings), comply with the building's regulations if any, and grant the landlord access for inspections or works. Failure to pay more than two months' rent exposes the tenant to judicial termination for serious breach with possible eviction, after a formal notice that remained unheeded.
bailHabitation.callout2Body: The landlord cannot pass on to the tenant: management or professional syndic fees beyond the tenant's share, major replacement works (boiler, roof, facade), property tax, home insurance other than building liability, or improvement/modernisation expenses.
bailHabitation.section4P1: The tenant may terminate at any time by registered letter with 3 months' notice (Art. 12 of the 2006 law). The landlord may only terminate with 6 months' notice and only for three legitimate reasons: personal occupancy need for themselves, spouse, ascendants or descendants; serious breach of contractual obligations by the tenant; demolition or reconstruction works making occupation impossible. Termination must be motivated in writing, on penalty of nullity.
bailHabitation.section4P2: In case of dispute (excessive rent, contested charges, unreturned deposit, contested inventory), the tenant or landlord may refer free of charge to the municipal Rent Commission of the dwelling's location (Art. 7 of the 2006 law). The Commission issues a non-binding opinion often followed by judges. If the opinion is ignored, the matter may be brought before the justice of the peace, or the district court for high rents.
bailHabitation.callout3Body: If several tenants sign together (cohabitation, flat-sharing), a solidarity clause makes each one potentially liable for the entire unpaid rent. After a co-tenant's departure, their solidarity cannot be maintained beyond a reasonable period (generally 6 months) without explicit consent — any clause to the contrary is void.

faq.q: What is the notice period to leave a rental in Luxembourg?
faq.a: The tenant gives 3 months' notice by registered letter (Art. 12 of the 2006 law). The landlord gives 6 months' notice and may only terminate for legitimate reasons (personal need, serious breach, major works).

faq.q: What is the maximum rental deposit in Luxembourg?
faq.a: The deposit is capped at 3 months' rent excluding charges (Art. 5 of the 2006 law). It must be placed in a blocked account in the tenant's name and interest belongs to the tenant. Any clause exceeding this is void.

faq.q: Can the landlord raise the rent during the lease?
faq.a: Revision is allowed only once every two years, capped by the STATEC consumer price index, or if improvement works justify a re-evaluation of the invested capital (with re-evaluation of the 5% cap). Increases must be notified by registered letter with one month's notice.

faq.q: What charges can be billed in addition to rent?
faq.a: Only those listed in the Grand Ducal Regulation of 16 June 2015: water, electricity and gas of common areas, collective heating, routine common area maintenance (cleaning, gardening, elevator), municipal waste tax and building liability insurance. Everything else (major works, syndic, property tax) is borne by the landlord.

faq.q: How to challenge an excessive rent?
faq.a: Refer free of charge to your municipality's Rent Commission. It checks the revalued invested capital calculation and issues an opinion. If the landlord refuses to comply, you can bring the case before the justice of the peace, who can order a retroactive rent reduction.

faq.q: What if the landlord does not return the deposit?
faq.a: Send a formal notice by registered letter first. Without reply within 30 days, refer to the Rent Commission or directly to the justice of the peace. The judge may order restitution plus interest and damages. Keep the exit inventory as evidence.
